newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's LDP can last unless economy falters - oppo.
newsitem.headline: Japan's LDP can last unless economy falters - oppo.

text.p: Japan's conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) can probably cling to power in a minority government unless the economy suffers a sudden shock, the leader of the main opposition party said on Wednesday.

"As long as the economy stays as it is, not doing well but but not falling into a situation that directly hits people's livelihoods, they can probably stay in power," Ichiro Ozawa, head of the Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
Should there be a sudden blow to the economy, however, "this kind of administration couldn't last", he added.

LDP officials said on Wednesday the party, which lifted its seats in an October 20 election but fell 12 short of a majority, was likely to form a minority government after failing to lure potential partners into a coalition.
The party was expected to try to keep a loose alliance with its two former partners, the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party, through a policy forum outside the cabinet.

"As long as all they try to do is stay in power...they can probably continue," said Ozawa, a long-time rival of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto who bolted the LDP in 1993 to act as key strategist for the reformist coalition which ended the long-ruling party's monopoly on power in August that year.
Less than a year later, the LDP was back, linked in a bizarre alliance with its former rivals, the Socialists.

Ozawa's own campaign calls for a freeze on Japan's three percent sales tax plus cuts in income and corporate taxes to boost the economy failed to convince many voters, and his party ended up with 156 seats, four fewer than before the poll.
But he said government policies that relied on a weak yen, low interest rates and more public spending to ensure recovery were unlikely to work.

"There is a possibility that the yen will crash," Ozawa said. "Given that Japan imports many things...inflation could emerge, the economy falter and the worst possible situation develop. Economic recovery will be difficand interest rates and on added public works spending."

The yen fell within a hair's breadth of 115 to the dollar on Tuesday, its lowest level since April 1993. It has rebounded a bit, but the outlook remains bearish given expectations Japanese interest rates will stay at rock-bottom levels.

Ozawa said an LDP government was unlikely to implement the drastic structural reforms and deregulation the economy needs to ensure future growth. "Basically they think that a regulated society is just fine and see no need to change," he said.

His own party has been in some disarray since the election, although it has so far averted a split that looked imminent soon after the vote. On Wednesday evening, reporters were gathered at party headquarters seeking news of defections.

Ozawa declined to be drawn on how many Shinshinto members he expected ultimately to leave the party fold. "If they think the Shinshinto is no good, then it's fine if they go their own way. But Ilarge number," he said.
